You are the Orchestrator in an autonomous optimization loop. Design one causal
experiment; do not edit candidate code, rebuild environments, run implementation
tests, or launch benchmarks.

## Authoritative inputs

- Objective: `/home/operator/dev/vibesys-runs/bad-cpp/.vibesys/state/runs/20260901-160434-429a8605-bad-cpp-20260901-160433/runtime/effective-objective.md`
- Progress ledger: `progress.md`
- Roadmap: `roadmap.md`
- Pareto archive: `pareto-frontier.md`
Read the objective first; every operator constraint is hard feasibility.
Accuracy, Pareto gain, or diagnostic value cannot excuse a violation. Cite
paths, not stable text. Then inspect the latest relevant ledger/roadmap entries;
search older work only when it can change the decision.

## Decision contract

Keep separate: (1) hard feasibility under every declared constraint and trusted
gate; (2) variance-aware Pareto retention of any feasible nondominated tradeoff;
and (3) terminal completion by one point satisfying every objective at once.

Expected effect is a forecast, not a rejection threshold. Separately define a
minimum from noise, cost, complexity, and allowed tradeoffs. A stronger
hypothesis diagnostic may block causal support but cannot erase a genuine
nondominated row unless it exposes a declared-contract violation.

Choose the frontier parent whose gap matches the mechanism. Set
`revert_to_round` when needed; the framework restores code and preserves memory.
Reuse trustworthy retained controls; remeasure only for concrete drift.

Profiler findings and suggestions are advisory, not prerequisites. Missing or
uncalibrated capture is uncertainty, not evidence that optimization must stop.
Turn a capability gap into instrumentation-only candidate work only when the
objective requests profiling or a quantitative comparison shows that capture is
the cheapest decision-changing experiment; otherwise preserve the gap and use a
direct causal A/B or bounded structural experiment.

## Strategy and roadmap

Update the roadmap concisely and select one active Major. Statuses: `todo` (not
started), `in_progress` (active), `done` (proved complete), `parked` (credible
direction, defective implementation), or `abandoned` (mechanism cannot help
this workload; a flat metric alone is insufficient). A blocker Minor names its
Major. Do not copy round history into the roadmap; seed 3-5 distinct Majors only
when it is nearly empty.

Classify the comparable trajectory; name its end-to-end delta, remaining gap,
and changed architecture boundary. After repeated noise, regressions, or
insufficient gains, compare useful-work/algorithm, device-execution, and
runtime/process/component changes, including a bounded structural option.
Once evidence clearly ranks one parent and mechanism, stop searching; another
lookup must be capable of changing the parent, mechanism, falsifier, or gate.

After a fair falsification or measured endpoints bound a tuning family, do not
interpolate another point only to map the Pareto frontier. Continue that family
only when a quantitative model shows a plausible simultaneous terminal crossing
within uncertainty, or the point resolves a named decision that changes the next
design. Otherwise pivot to a structural mechanism. This governs experiment
selection, not retention of genuine nondominated rows.


## Task granularity and design freedom

The external contract is fixed; language, runtime, process topology, build,
executable layout, and component boundaries remain design variables unless an
authoritative input restricts them. Scope limits uncertainty, not diff size.

Return one stable hypothesis with causal claim, activation evidence, falsifier,
analytical effect range, separately justified minimum, and a causally complete
task. Keep the handoff under 4,000 output tokens: `invariants` cites stable files
and adds only hypothesis diagnostics; `task` states the component/interface and
stages without an exhaustive shell recipe; `pass_criteria` adds only activation,
correctness, cleanup, and evidence gates; `reasoning` gives the decisive
comparison and rejected alternatives briefly.

Include in `task` a verification strategy: the cheapest checks the implementer
should run before declaring the work done. These are not exhaustive test plans;
they are the minimum steps that exercise the failure-prone path (e.g. "confirm
the image builds," "hit /health and get 200," "run the accuracy checker against
the live endpoint"). Adapt the strategy across retries based on what failed.

Stage cost: cheap capability, comparable point, then expand past noise.
Stop on fair falsification; reuse plumbing/rows. State hard paid-call maxima
over retries. A wrapper rejected before target allocation is
unspent only with raw proof no target phase began. The framework owns official
gates, rollback, review cadence, and terminal detection.
After a correctness failure, cover changed dataflow locally or stagewise isolate
defects before another target call; leaf-only checks do not suffice.

The framework has a machine-readable trusted benchmark and runs it after review.
Do not ask the implementer to duplicate that canonical command.

Official evaluation runs every 3 accepted
candidates, on request, and finally. Provisional count:
0; cadence is
not due. Request
early when delay blocks a decision, especially after changing the served
process/listener/entrypoint; an internal controller cannot prove deployment.
Its production startup must select the retained arm. If an A/B candidate fails
but its control is retained, do not leave the failed arm as an implicit default.

## Skills

Recommend zero or more narrow installed skill references with a purpose. Do not
preload them or make an allowlist; the implementer may discover others.


Return only the schema-valid JSON object. The framework records the plan and
continues until the configured round budget ends.

tool_result.content:
# Objective: minimize badgraph's total benchmark time

Make the graph library in this repository faster. The scored metric is
`total_ms` from `./bin/bench --scale 1.0 --json <path>`: the summed wall-clock
time of all benchmarks. Lower is better. Find the bottlenecks yourself, from
profiling and measurement.

## Hard constraints

1. **The correctness gate must stay green.** `./bin/tests` recomputes every
   expected value with independent reference implementations. Any red test
   invalidates the round regardless of the benchmark number.
2. **Benchmark checksums must not change.** Every benchmark prints and records
   `sum=0x...` over its real output. A changed checksum means the optimization
   altered observable results or silently dropped work; that is a failure, not
   a speedup.
3. **All benchmarks must remain present in the JSON output.** Removing or
   renaming a benchmark to shrink `total_ms` is not an optimization.
4. **Workload parameters are fixed.** Do not change benchmark sizes, `--scale`
   handling, repetition counts, or the timing methodology in
   `bench/bench.cpp` to make numbers smaller. Changes to `bench/bench.cpp`
   are allowed only when an API change in the library forces a matching
   call-site update, and must preserve workloads and checksums.
5. **The build stays a plain portable `make` build.** Binaries must still be
   produced at `bin/bench` and `bin/tests`; no hardware-specific flags that
   break on other machines; `-Wall` stays.

Everything else — algorithms, data layout, memory management, API shape (with
matching test and bench call-site updates), build flags within the rules
above — is fair game.

result.activation_evidence: `./bin/bench --scale 1.0 --json bench_results.json` after the change, compared row-by-row against `baseline.json` (total 1547.07 ms): each rewritten benchmark's `ms` drops while its `checksum` string is identical. Expected direction per row — string_churn 285.6, topo_naive 262.1, critical_path 298.1, lca_naive 144.1, topo_kahn 110.0, bfs_levels 83.8, topo_dfs 71.9 all strictly lower; build_tree, subtree_sum_all, pointer_chase (untouched code paths) within noise. `python3 tools/compare.py baseline.json bench_results.json` prints `ok` on all ten rows and exits 0. No `NONDETERMINISTIC` appears in any note. These are the only implementations linked into `bin/bench`, so a time drop on exactly the rewritten rows is direct activation proof.
result.expected_effect: total_ms 1547.07 → 250–500 ms (3.1–6.2x). Per row: string_churn 285.6→<10 (linear append), topo_naive 262.1→<5 (ordered-ready selection), lca_naive 144.1→<5 (O(depth) set membership), topo_kahn 110.0→<15, bfs_levels 83.8→<15 (O(1) FIFO pop), critical_path 298.1→<40 (same FIFO fix, twice per rep, plus its `std::map` dist scan remaining), topo_dfs 71.9→<40 (no per-level path copy; `std::set` marker cost remains). Untouched: build_tree 48.1, subtree_sum_all 176.8, pointer_chase 66.6 — roughly 290 ms of irreducible residue this round, which is the entry point for the M2/M3 container and layout Majors.
result.falsification_criteria: The hypothesis is falsified if, with the rewrites in place and checksums unchanged, the targeted benchmarks each move by less than 5% (i.e. the quadratic terms were not the cost — the compiler was already eliding them, or the time is really in the `std::map`/pointer-chase layer that this round does not touch), or if `total_ms` falls by less than 25% overall. It is also falsified as stated — and must be reported as such rather than patched around — if any rewrite that is argued to be output-preserving turns out to change a checksum, since that means the emission order or FP summation order is not in fact determined by the property the rewrite relies on.
result.hypothesis: Seven of the ten benchmarks are dominated not by container constants but by accidental superlinear work inside `src/toposort.cpp` and `src/algos.cpp`: `describeHot` rebuilds the entire report string per emitted line (O(bytes^2) copying, 1.26 MB output), `topoSortKahnSlow` and `bfsLevels` pop their FIFO with `vector::erase(begin())` (O(n^2) memmove at n=90000), `topoSortNaive` recounts indegrees by scanning the whole adjacency map per emitted node (O(n^2·E)), `lcaNaive` linear-scans the ancestor path at every step up from `b` (O(depth^2) on a 5000-deep chain), and `dfsVisit` copies its `ancestors` vector at every recursion level. Each of these has a rewrite that emits a byte-identical output sequence, so replacing them with linear/log-linear equivalents removes work that is pure overhead and cuts `total_ms` several-fold with every checksum unchanged.
result.invariants:
Hard constraints are in `.vibesys/state/runs/20260901-160434-429a8605-bad-cpp-20260901-160433/runtime/effective-objective.md`; reference behaviour is defined by `tests/test_graph.cpp` and the recorded checksums in `baseline.json`. Hypothesis-specific invariants the implementer must hold, each of which is a real trap here:

1. Output *sequence* must be preserved, not just the set. `checksum(vector<int>)` folds elements in order, so any reordering of a topo order or BFS level vector changes the sum even when the result is still valid. `tests/test_graph.cpp:151-166` only checks validity and set equality, so tests passing does **not** imply checksums hold — the bench checksum is the strict gate.
2. `topoSortNaive`'s selection rule is "the lowest-numbered still-present node whose current indegree over still-present sources is zero" (`ids()` returns ascending keys from a `std::map`). A decrement-based scheme must pick the minimum ready id, count duplicate edges with multiplicity (`makeRandomDag` can add the same pair twice), leave a self-loop node permanently unready, and stop early with a short output when nothing is ready — all reproducing today's `if (pick < 0) break;`.
3. `topoSortKahnSlow` and `bfsLevels` are FIFO; only the pop cost may change, never the push order. `bfsLevels` emits one entry per node in `nodeMap()` order with `-1` for unreached nodes.
4. `dfsVisit`'s by-value `ancestors` is exactly the current root-to-node path; a by-reference version must push before descending and pop after, and keep both early-returns and the post-order `done.insert`/`out.push_back` in place.
5. Floating-point summation order must not change. `checksum(vector<double>)` quantizes at 1e-3, which is a small cushion, not a licence to reassociate; `longestPathDag` and `subtreeSum` are out of scope this round precisely so this does not have to be argued.
6. Do not modify `bench/bench.cpp`, `tests/test_graph.cpp`, `Makefile`, or `baseline.json`. No API change is needed for this round; `include/badgraph.hpp` should not need to change either.
result.minimum_acceptance_criteria: Retain only if all ten checksums are byte-identical to `baseline.json`, `./bin/tests` is fully green, and `total_ms` at scale 1.0 is at least 25% below 1547.07 ms (≤1160 ms). Justification, separate from the forecast: the harness reports best-of-3 and `tools/compare.py` treats ±10% as noise, so 25% is ~2.5x the declared noise band and well clear of it; the change touches two source files with no API or build change, so implementation cost is low and no tradeoff axis other than `total_ms` is configured — there is nothing to trade away. A result between 5% and 25% means the quadratic terms were real but minor and should be reported with the per-row numbers rather than retried, since that redirects the next round to M2 rather than to more of M1.
result.pass_criteria:
Activation: `bench_results.json` at scale 1.0 shows strictly lower `ms` than `baseline.json` for string_churn, topo_naive, topo_kahn, critical_path, bfs_levels, lca_naive, and topo_dfs; the per-row before/after table is included in the report.

Correctness: `./bin/tests` emits no `FAIL` line; `python3 tools/compare.py baseline.json bench_results.json` exits 0 with all ten rows marked `ok` and no row `MISSING` or `(new)`; every checksum string matches `baseline.json` exactly; no benchmark note contains `NONDETERMINISTIC`.

Constraint compliance: `git diff` touches only `src/toposort.cpp` and `src/algos.cpp` — `bench/bench.cpp`, `tests/test_graph.cpp`, `Makefile`, and `baseline.json` are unmodified; `make -s all` succeeds with `-Wall` and produces `bin/bench` and `bin/tests`; no new compiler flags, no hardware-specific flags, no new external dependency.

Cleanup: no debug printing left in library code, no temporary files added to the tree, no commented-out old implementations left behind.

Evidence: the report states, per rewritten routine, the property that makes it output-preserving (selection rule, FIFO order, path semantics, or byte-for-byte append), and reports the achieved `total_ms` against the 1160 ms acceptance bound. If a routine was dropped after a checksum failure, say which and what the checksum did.
result.reasoning:
Round 1 with an empty ledger and one frontier axis (`total_ms`), so the only question is which mechanism buys the most measured time per unit of risk. Reading `src/` against `baseline.json` splits the 1547 ms into two separable families: accidental superlinear work (~1255 ms across seven rows) and container/layout constants (~290 ms residue). M1 wins the comparison on every dimension that matters here — it is the larger share, it needs no API change so `tests/test_graph.cpp` and `bench/bench.cpp` stay untouched (removing the main route to a constraint violation), and each rewrite has an independently checkable output-preserving argument that `--only <name>` can verify in isolation for pennies.

Rejected: M2, the dense id-indexed core, as the round-1 parent — it is the obvious "root cause" framing, but it must change `nodeMap()`/`adjacency()` and therefore edit the correctness gate's own call sites in the same round the gate is the only arbiter, and it would not touch string_churn (285 ms) or topo_naive (262 ms) at all, since those are quadratic in output bytes and in rescans rather than in lookup cost. It is strictly better done second, against a baseline where the quadratic terms no longer mask the layout signal. Rejected: M5 build flags (`-O3`/LTO) — cheap, but a uniform constant-factor shift applied first would contaminate the per-row attribution for every later mechanism. Rejected: an instrumentation-only profiling round — the objective asks for profiling, but the bench harness already reports per-benchmark timings with checksums, the cost structure is legible by inspection, and a direct A/B against `baseline.json` is the cheaper decision-changing experiment; the capability gap is preserved rather than spent.

No revert: round 1 has no parent to restore.
result.task:
Rewrite the superlinear routines in `src/toposort.cpp` and `src/algos.cpp` so each emits a byte-identical output sequence in linear or log-linear time. Public API in `include/badgraph.hpp` stays as it is; internal data structures inside these functions are free. Scope is exactly these six call sites — `describeHot`, `topoSortNaive`, `topoSortKahnSlow`, `topoSortDfsRecursive`/`dfsVisit`, `bfsLevels`, `lcaNaive`. Leave `subtreeSum`/`subtreeSumAll`, `longestPathDag`, `totalWeight`, and the generators alone; they are the next Major and mixing them in would blur the evidence.

The intended rewrites: `describeHot` appends in place instead of assigning a rebuilt string (`report += line`, `line += ...`), optionally reserving; `topoSortKahnSlow` and `bfsLevels` keep their FIFO push order but pop with a head index or a deque instead of `erase(begin())`, and may use id-indexed storage for the indegree/level tables in place of `std::map` where ids permit; `topoSortNaive` maintains live indegrees and selects the minimum ready id from an ordered structure, decrementing out-neighbours on removal, instead of rescanning the adjacency map; `dfsVisit` takes `ancestors` by reference with push/pop around the recursion; `lcaNaive` builds a membership structure over `pathA` once per query and walks `b` upward testing membership, instead of a linear scan per step.

Staged execution — do one routine at a time, cheapest and most isolated first (`describeHot`, then the two FIFO pops, then `lcaNaive`, then `dfsVisit`, then `topoSortNaive`), and do not start the next until the current one is verified.

Verification strategy, run after each stage (the whole suite is ~2 s at scale 1.0, so there is no reason to batch):
- `make -s all` — must build clean; `-Wall` stays and no new warnings may appear.
- `./bin/tests` — must print zero `FAIL` lines. Run this after *every* stage, not only at the end.
- `./bin/bench --scale 1.0 --only <name> --json /tmp/stage.json` and diff that row's `checksum` against the same row in `baseline.json`. A changed checksum means the equivalence argument for that rewrite is wrong: revert that one routine, re-derive the argument, and only then retry. Do not proceed with a red checksum.
- Once all six are in: `./bin/bench --scale 1.0 --json bench_results.json` then `python3 tools/compare.py baseline.json bench_results.json`, which must exit 0 with all ten rows `ok`.
- `git diff --stat` to confirm only `src/toposort.cpp` and `src/algos.cpp` changed.

Cost ceiling: local runs are cheap, so verify liberally; but cap this round at two full re-attempts after a correctness failure. If a second attempt on the same routine still moves a checksum, drop that one routine from the change, keep the verified rest, and report which one was dropped and why — a partial pass with an honest account is worth more than a red gate.

Report back: the full `bench_results.json`, the `compare.py` output, the per-row before/after table against `baseline.json`, and one sentence per routine stating the property that makes the rewrite output-preserving.

## Where the run actually is

Round 1 of a **single-round run** (`max_rounds: 1` in `_vibesys_chat/trajectory/state/run.json`). The last event is seq 52 at `16:08:45Z` — the orchestrator's `StructuredOutput` call closing `round-1-plan`. There's no `phase_started` for an implement phase yet, and `git status --porcelain` shows only `progress.md`, `roadmap.md`, and an untracked `progress-artifacts/plans/`. **No source file has been touched.** The plan just landed; nothing is fixed yet.

(Side note: `bench_results.json` in the tree is stale — it's a scale-0.25 run with mtime 09:02, two minutes *before* the run started. It is not a round-1 result.)

## The diagnosis — which I checked against `src/`, not just the plan

The baseline is 1547.07 ms across 10 benchmarks. Six routines account for ~1255 ms of it, and every one is accidental superlinearity rather than a constant factor:

| Site | Defect | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| `src/algos.cpp:182` `describeHot` | `report = report + line + "\n"` rebuilds the whole report per line — O(bytes²) over 1.26 MB | string_churn 285.6 |
| `src/toposort.cpp:44` `topoSortKahnSlow` | `ready.erase(ready.begin())` — O(n²) memmove at n=90000 | topo_kahn 110.0, and critical_path 298.1 calls it twice per rep |
| `src/algos.cpp:95` `bfsLevels` | same `erase(begin())` FIFO pop | bfs_levels 83.8 |
| `src/toposort.cpp:18-27` `topoSortNaive` | recounts indegree by scanning the *entire* adjacency map per emitted node — O(n²·E) | topo_naive 262.1 (at n=3500!) |
| `src/algos.cpp:20-23` `lcaNaive` | linear-scans `pathA` at every step up from `b` — O(depth²) on a 5000-deep chain | lca_naive 144.1 |
| `src/toposort.cpp:65` `dfsVisit` | takes `ancestors` **by value** at every recursion level | topo_dfs 71.9 |

## The process

Staged, one routine at a time, cheapest-and-most-isolated first: `describeHot` → the two FIFO pops → `lcaNaive` → `dfsVisit` → `topoSortNaive`. After *each* stage: `make -s all` clean under `-Wall`, `./bin/tests` with zero FAILs, and `./bin/bench --scale 1.0 --only <name>` with that row's checksum diffed against `baseline.json`. A moved checksum means the equivalence argument was wrong — revert that one routine, re-derive, retry at most twice, then drop it and report honestly rather than patch around it.

Scope is deliberately narrow: two files, no API change, so `tests/test_graph.cpp` and `bench/bench.cpp` stay untouched — which removes the main route to a constraint violation. Acceptance is all ten checksums byte-identical, tests green, and `total_ms ≤ 1160` (25% below baseline, ~2.5× the harness's declared 10% noise band). Forecast is 250–500 ms.

Deferred on purpose: the dense id-indexed graph core (M2), node payload layout (M3), redundancy elimination (M4), and `-O3`/LTO (M5). M5 is held back specifically so a uniform constant-factor shift doesn't contaminate per-row attribution for the structural work.

## What I'd flag

**The checksum gate is strictly stronger than the test gate, and `topoSortNaive` is where that bites.** `checksum(vector<int>)` folds in order, so any reordering of a valid topo order changes the sum — while `tests/test_graph.cpp` only checks validity and set equality. Reading the current loop, its selection rule is implicit and has four traps a decrement-based rewrite must reproduce: pick the *lowest-numbered* ready id; count duplicate edges **with multiplicity** (the inner loop increments per matching entry, and `makeRandomDag` can add a pair twice); leave self-loop nodes permanently unready; and break early with a short output when nothing is ready. The plan does list these as invariants, which is the right call — but it's the one rewrite where "obviously equivalent" isn't.

Second, smaller: the objective says to find bottlenecks "from profiling and measurement," and the plan explicitly rejected an instrumentation round in favor of reading the code against the per-benchmark timings the harness already reports. Defensible given how legible the cost structure is, but it's a judgment call against the letter of the objective, and with `max_rounds: 1` there's no second round to revisit it in.

judge_result.feedback:
Non-blocking — these do NOT affect the PASS and require no rework of this round. Carry them into the next round.

1. `src/toposort.cpp:6-13` and `src/algos.cpp:8-15` — the `maxNodeId()` comment states "every id in nodeMap() or in an adjacency list lies in [0, maxNodeId(g)]" as unconditional. It is false: `Graph::removeNode` leaves one copy of a duplicated consecutive edge behind (because `Graph::removeEdge` increments `i` after `erase`, skipping the shifted element), and `Graph::compact()` erases dead leaves without removing incoming edges. Either can leave an adjacency target above `maxNodeId()`. I reproduced a `heap-buffer-overflow` in `topoSortNaive` under ASan with: 3 nodes, `addEdge(0,2)` twice, `removeNode(2)`; the same probe against parent `41e249c` runs clean, so this is a regression the flat tables introduced. `topoSortKahnSlow`, `bfsLevels`, and `dfsVisit` share the exposure. It does not block because neither `removeNode` nor `compact` is reachable from `bench/bench.cpp` or `tests/test_graph.cpp`, and I confirmed both binaries are ASan-clean. Fix cheaply by sizing the tables to `max(maxNodeId, largest adjacency target)` or bounds-guarding the target index, and correct the comment to state the precondition rather than assert the invariant. This matters most for M2 (dense id-indexed core), which would propagate the same false premise across `nodeMap()`/`adjacency()`.

2. `progress-artifacts/round-0001/validation-recipe.json` — `input_paths` omits `bench/bench.cpp`, but the recipe command runs `make all`, which builds `bin/bench` from it. Add it so the path set fully determines whether a prior passing result can be reused.

3. Optional coverage note: the differential harness's `sparse-ids-after-removeNode` case uses only single (non-duplicated) edges, which is exactly the case that cannot trigger finding 1. If you keep the harness for M2, add a duplicate-edge + `removeNode` case and run it under `-fsanitize=address`.

candidate source, reading only enough to judge whether measurement would change
the first plan.

The framework can run `macos_cpu` profiling through its
`local` capture path. Request only evidence
that path can observe. Do not request a different profiler. If the needed
discriminator is outside its visibility, skip profiling and record that
capability gap in your reasoning for the design call.
Treat this declared capability as authoritative; do not audit profiler source
or design new capture infrastructure in this phase.

Request profiling when current source/history cannot locate the next mechanism,
a comparable flat/regressed result needs attribution, or one measured
bottleneck would change hypothesis ranking. State the exact focus and smallest
discriminating capture.

Skip profiling when static evidence or a recent comparable profile already
determines the next step, when the current defect needs a local repair, or when
the workspace contains terminal edits and planning must first select/restore a
trusted checkpoint. This phase cannot apply rollback.

Profiling measures a running system, and round 1 has no prior result saying one
exists. A pinned seed checkout or a declared benchmark contract states intent,
not the state of this workspace, so despite the restriction above you may run
one cheap check to settle it; leave no long-lived process behind and never
stand in for a benchmark run.

If it does not build or run, no profile is possible however useful its evidence
would be: set `need_profile=false` and record that the next round's work is to
make it run. If it does run, decide on evidentiary value alone, weighing that
round 1 holds no measurement at all, so a profile is the only way this
campaign's first plan can target a measured bottleneck rather than a guessed
one. If the check is inconclusive, prefer `need_profile=false`: a skipped
profile costs one round of unmeasured planning, while profiling a candidate
that does not run spends an expensive turn on a summary with no measurement
behind it.

Return only the schema-valid JSON object.

Optimize a single-producer, single-consumer bounded FIFO queue.

Headline metric: `total_ops_per_sec` (maximize).

Preserve the required interface:
- Provide a native shared library named `./queue-candidate.so`.
- Export the evaluator's copying C ABI.
- Implement enqueue and dequeue for copied byte values using the capacity and
  value size supplied by the trusted runner.

The candidate may use any language or combination of languages. The queue must
remain linearizable, must not fabricate or duplicate items, and must respect
capacity. Maximize trusted end-to-end operation throughput for the SPSC
workload.

Start from the editable Rust implementation in `src/lib.rs`. It is an
intentionally naive correctness baseline, not part of the trusted evaluator.

result.reasoning: Cheap check confirms the candidate builds and runs (run-init dylib exports all 9 vsq_* symbols; dlopen probe returned abi=1 and STATUS_OK for queue/producer/consumer create), so a profile is technically possible — my own cargo EPERM was a shell TMPDIR restriction, not a workspace defect. But static evidence already determines round 1's plan: the baseline is Mutex<VecDeque<Vec<u8>>> with a per-enqueue heap allocation and per-dequeue free, stacking mutex contention, allocator traffic, and pointer indirection on an SPSC path, and all three are removed by the same single structural rewrite to a preallocated cache-line-padded lock-free ring over a flat capacity*max_value_size slab. A macos_cpu sample would show time in pthread_mutex_lock and malloc, confirming rather than reranking the hypothesis, and would attribute cost in code the first Major deletes wholesale. The profile with real discriminating power (false sharing vs payload memcpy vs atomic ordering) is round 2, against the ring implementation.
